morph.stmt: Largely isolating with a small mixed affix inventory: 'Some verbs are inflected for person and number through prefixes, and intransitive verbs sometimes get subject agreement suffixes. Adjectives, pronouns, and in some dialects demonstratives and numerals get a suffix -n' (abstract p.2); possessors are suffixes, Adonara additionally has object suffixes (p.43), while derivation is by fossilised prefixes be-, ke-, pe(N)-, meN-, N- and infix -en- ('Most of them are no longer productive', p.34; -n 'is the only clearly identifiable suffix', p.37); reduplication is treated apart from affixation…

826.heavy: 'a closed final syllable of the stem in Adyghe always carries stress' (Borise 2018: 13, citing Rogava & Kerasheva 1966: 25); secondary-sourced -- primary pp. 23-24, 26 do not phrase a closed-syllable rule (p. 24 states instead that in nouns/stative verbs a final open ə-syllable is apparently always stressed; p. 26 describes final-vowel syncope).
826.dflt: Primary (Arkadiev et al. 2009: 23): stress 'usually on the last, more rarely on the penultimate syllable of the wordform' -- a dominant-final tendency, not a categorical default; which of the two is partly unpredictable / set by part of speech (Borise). Abzakh dialect: generally final (Paris 1989).
826.prule: Standard (Temirgoy-based) / literary and Shapsugh West Circassian: stress 'usually on the last, more rarely on the penultimate syllable of the wordform' (Arkadiev et al. 2009: 23), but the counting domain is the STEM, morphologically defined: certain tense suffixes, absolutive prefixes, demonstratives and the 3rd-person possessive count as stem, while the 'endings' (case, number, 1st/2nd possessive, emphatic -ba etc.) are stress-invisible, so stress can stand 3rd or 4th from the word end (sə-k’wá-ʁɐ-ba 'I did go'); 1st/2nd person prefixes apparently pull stress leftward (s-é-ḳwe 'I go' vs ma-ḳwé 'he goes'). Within the stem-final two-syllable window: a closed stem-final syllable always takes stress (Borise < Rogava & Kerasheva 1966: 25); in nouns and stative verbs a final open ə-syllable is apparently always stressed (unstressed final -ə having dropped), whereas dynamic verbs allow final unstressed -ə; otherwise ultima vs penult is partly unpredictable and partly set by part of speech (noun/verb minimal pairs wéš’xə 'you laugh' vs weš’xə́ 'rain'). Abzakh dialect: stress generally word-final (Paris 1989: 165-166).
826.srule: Not mentioned in Arkadiev et al. 2009, sec. 2 pp. 23-24 (whole prosody passage read; also absent from Arkadiev & Lander 2018 sec. 2.4 and Borise 2018 sec. 6.1.1 for Adyghe). 830.dq: Aguaruna has a pitch accent: in every phonological word, one syllable carries an accent, and is pronounced with a higher pitch than the rest of the word. The principle of “one word per accent, one accent per word” is an important criterion and diagnostic of wordhood (§2.8).

830.prule: Culminative pitch accent: exactly one accented (high-pitched) syllable nucleus per phonological word. Position is lexically specified on roots and (verbal) suffixes; in verbs the leftmost underlying accent surfaces, default = second vowel of an unaccented disyllabic root; in nouns/adjectives accent is lexical (disyllables overwhelmingly initial, trisyllables generally second syllable) and most nominal suffixes shift accent one syllable rightward. Accent is phonemically contrastive (minimal pairs). No stress system separate from the pitch accent is described.
830.srule: None within the word: “one word per accent, one accent per word”; 'There is one primary accent per word' (Overall 2007 §2.7 p.96, §2.8 p.108). 843.dq: In other cases, stress is automatically determined by tone. Except as noted in those sections, stress occurs with the following tones: The first high tone of a series of one or more ... In general, the actual volume of stressed vowels appears to decrease throughout an utterance as does the pitch of high tones.
843.prule: Three tone phonemes (high, mid = downstepped high, low; terraced-level with downdrift). Stress is not an independent word-level system: it is 'automatically determined by tone' — the first high tone of a series is stressed (strongest), the first low of an initial low series gets a lesser stress, mid tones have zero stress; residual non-automatic stress is analysed as a marker of juncture (break) rather than as phonemic stress.
843.srule: Lesser, tone-determined stresses (Welmers 1946): a stress weaker than the first-high-tone stress falls on the first low tone of an initial series of two or more lows and on an initial single low tone (not on an initial vowel); a still weaker stress on the second low of a low series after a high tone, and a weak stress on a mid tone following a low tone. Placement follows the tone string within juncture-delimited series, not syllable count; no alternating rhythm is described.

evidence_works.detail: Three production experiments on Asante Twi show that corrective focus lowers the pitch register of both H and L tones (in situ and ex situ), duration is not consistently affected, and givenness is not marked prosodically. On word prosody the article states that Akan is a two-tone (L, H) terraced-level language with downstep and syllable TBU, and that the only stress claim in the literature is Christaller's impressionistic distribution, which the authors treat as unverified and possibly an artefact of H tone.

845.dq: The stress in a disyllabic noun is always on the syllable with the highest tone irrespective of whether the syllable is an affix or not. If both syllables have the same tone, the stress is even.
845.dloc: Hansson 2003: p.241 (sec. 3 Word formation, final paragraph before sec. 4 Syntax); archive.org 'sino-tibetan-languages'
845.prule: Lexical tone system (three tones x two phonation types). The only stress statement makes stress derivative of tone: in a disyllabic noun stress falls on the syllable bearing the highest tone (affix or not); if both syllables carry the same tone, stress is even. No positional or weight-based word-stress rule.
845.srule: Hansson 2003 says nothing about secondary stress. Nishida 1966 (Saen Chai Akha, p.6): in a compound word the primary stress falls on the last syllable of the main word (on the syllable before it if that syllable is the bound morpheme -ɦɯ) and a secondary stress appears on the last syllable of the preceding word, e.g. [ʔu22ˌdu22 tʃʻa̰33ˈkʻõː55] 'hair of the head'.

846.dq: The following norms for word accentuation are reliably derived from indirect evidence ... Exceptions: word accent falls on a long final vowel resulting from contraction
846.heavy: a syllable 'is said to be long if it contains a long vowel or if it is closed by a consonant'; in addition a long final vowel resulting from contraction (circumflex, i.e. an ultraheavy final) attracts the accent
846.dflt: antepenult in words of three or more syllables; initial in disyllables (Caplice 1988 §4(8), p. 8)

851.dq: Each phonological word has a primary stress, and when words form a phonological phrase, the primary stress goes on the right-most word. Clitics are integrated into the phonological word, causing stress shift. (§3.2.1, p. 119); cf. §2.5.2 p. 108: 'what are the arguments to justify the occurrence of word-level stress to be presented?'

851.prule: Primary stress falls unpredictably on either the final or the penultimate syllable of the lexical word (right-edge two-syllable window); explicitly not sensitive to syllable weight; minimal pairs distinguished by stress alone ([ˈbago] 'dry' vs [baˈgo] 'ant sp.'). Author lists di- and trisyllables under both ULTIMATE and PENULTIMATE headings; notes 'No polysyllabic lexical words were found with ultimate stress' (4+ syllable words penultimate). Chapter summary nonetheless labels the language 'iambic... primary stress is assigned to the right-most foot of a word or phrase'. Clitics integrate into the phonological word and shift stress ([kaˈdo] 'necklace' -> [oˈkaɾʊ] 'my necklace'); in phrases/compounds primary stress goes to the right-most word.
851.srule: Only in compounds and phrases: the right-most component takes the primary stress and the stress of the preceding component is reduced to secondary (e.g. [oˌɾoɾoˈpɛ] 'clothes', [uˌtaˈnĩŋ] 'smoke'; phrase [aˌpaɾaˈka] '(he/she) eats bananas'). No word-internal rhythmic secondary stress is described; single words of up to four syllables carry one stress ([aɾaˈmĩɾa], [akaˈtaba]). (Aragon 2014, §2.4.5 p. 105, §2.5.2 pp. 108-113, §3.2.1 pp. 119-120 read.)

dfl.note: The grammar calls the final-vs-penult choice 'unpredictable' (§2.5.2 p. 111) but characterises the majority pattern as iambic (right-edge, i.e. final stress): 'most of the phonological words follow this same pattern of iambic stress' (§2.4.5 p. 105) and the chapter summary describes Akuntsú 'as an iambic language, where primary stress is assigned to the right-most foot of a word or phrase' (§2.6 p. 117); note that words of four or more syllables were found only with penultimate stress (p. 110).
dfl.q: Note that stress assignment is the same also for compounds. It is not a surprising effect of stress assignment in Akuntsú, since most of the phonological words follow this same pattern of iambic stress. ... Akuntsú was described as an iambic language, where primary stress is assigned to the right-most foot of a word or phrase.
